{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01FBRSzQdHax63aoC5EGnnj2","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Eval harness — rubric, test prompts, protocol\n2\t\n3\tMeasures whether a produced BUILD PLAN actually follows the skill. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_cpwlba2eq4ynjnb7qtmbnfzcm6efuvej4orbl4lkodb2vehrxl5a","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Multi-Tenant SaaS Billing System\n\n> **Interpretation:** I read this as the billing subsystem of a multi-tenant SaaS product, where we charge our tenants for subscriptions and usage. The other reading is a billing platform that other businesses use to charge their own customers. That version needs a second tenant level (merchant → end customer) and is hard to add later, so it's listed as a gate in §2 instead of being assumed.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Classification\n- **What:** A system that keeps the price catalog, manages subscriptions, meters usage, prices it, issues invoices, collects payments and runs retries on failed payments, for many tenants that share one platform.\n- **Type:** Software, plus infrastructure for usage ingestion. **No AI.**\n- **Dominant constraint:** **Correctness.** Money has to be exact, fully traceable and charged exactly once. Compliance comes second (PCI scope, tax, audit trail).\n- **Worst failure:** **Wrong money.** That means charging a tenant twice, using one tenant's data to bill another, or failing to record revenue without anyone noticing. All three destroy trust, and the third can go unseen for months.\n\n## 2. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Default (chosen now) | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Consistency vs availability** | **Split.** The ledger, invoices and payments need strong consistency: one Postgres primary, with ledger writes in serializable transactions. Usage ingestion stays available instead: it accepts events into a durable buffer even when the core database is down, and removes duplicates later. | Contractual multi-region active-active, or data residency rules. Answer with regional **cells**: each tenant is pinned to one region and keeps a consistent ledger there. Never use a globally distributed ledger. |\n| **Monolith vs services** | **Modular monolith.** One deployable with strict module boundaries (tenancy, catalog, subscriptions, metering, rating, invoicing, ledger, payments, dunning) and one Postgres. Modules talk only through their public interfaces, and a CI lint blocks imports across modules. | Usage ingestion stays above about 5k events/s, or ingestion deploys start blocking core billing deploys. Then split out **metering only**. Also flip when there are 3 or more teams with clashing release schedules. |\n| **Sync vs async** | **Sync** for API changes such as creating a subscription or changing a plan: the state change and its ledger entries go in one transaction. **Async**, through a transactional outbox, for billing runs, payment attempts, tax calls, emails and webhooks. Postgres `SKIP LOCKED` workers to start; no Kafka. | Checkout needs payment confirmation inline (for example a strict SCA flow). Then add a sync charge path for that endpoint only. Move to a broker when 3 or more independent consumers need fan-out and replay. |\n| **Build vs buy** | **Buy** payment processing (Stripe Payments with Elements, so cards never reach us and PCI scope stays at SAQ-A), tax (Stripe Tax or Avalara) and email (Postmark or SES). **Build** the ledger, subscriptions, rating and invoicing. The ledger is the source of truth, usage pricing will outgrow off-the-shelf models, and we don't want to depend on one processor. | If the real pricing sheet is only flat per-seat plans with no usage pricing, **buy the whole engine** (Stripe Billing, Chargebee or Orb). This plan then shrinks to integration plus a ledger copy. **Check this against the actual pricing sheet in week 1.** |\n| **Tenant isolation model** | **Shared database and shared schema.** Every row has `tenant_id`, enforced by **Postgres row-level security (RLS)** using a per-transaction `app.tenant_id` setting. The app's database role is not the table owner, so it cannot bypass RLS. | An enterprise contract requires a dedicated database, or a tenant creates noisy-neighbor load. Then move that tenant into a dedicated cell with the same schema and migrations. |\n| **Ledger model** | **Double-entry, append-only and immutable.** Corrections are made with reversing entries, never `UPDATE` or `DELETE` (a database trigger enforces this). Normal state tables sit beside it; this is not full event sourcing. | **Treat this as permanent.** The only flip is to full event sourcing, if a regulator or auditor needs every state rebuilt from scratch. |\n| **Money representation** | `bigint` minor units plus an ISO 4217 currency code. No floats anywhere. Rounding rules (banker's or half-up, per currency) live in one place. Each price list is set in one currency; **no FX conversion**. | A tenant must be billed in a currency that has no price list. Then add an FX rate table and record the rate used on each invoice. |\n| **Tenant hierarchy** | One level: **tenant = billed customer**, with billing accounts below it. | We sell billing to other businesses. Then add a merchant → customer hierarchy with per-merchant processor accounts (Stripe Connect). Decide this before Phase 1 because every table changes. |\n| **Region / residency** | Single region (for example `us-east-1`) spread across zones. RPO 5 min or less, RTO 4 h or less. | The first EU-residency contract, or a region-level RTO under 1 h. Then add an EU cell. |\n| **(AI) prompt+RAG vs fine-tune** | N/A: there are no model-driven features. | An AI feature is proposed. Re-run this skill for that feature. |\n| **(AI) hosted API vs self-host** | N/A, same reason. | Same. |\n\n## 3. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n\n**The one real request:** `POST /v1/subscriptions` for one internal tenant (`acme-internal`) on one hard-coded plan (`starter`, $1.00/month, USD), followed by a real live-mode charge to a company card. The charge is refunded afterwards.\n\n**Real response:** `201` with the subscription ID. Then, asynchronously: invoice `INV-0001` is finalized, Stripe charges $1.00, the `payment_intent.succeeded` webhook comes back, and the invoice is marked `paid`. The ledger ends up balanced: accounts receivable, cash and deferred revenue entries net to zero.\n\n**Tiers it crosses:**\n1. Edge: ALB with TLS and AWS WAF.\n2. API: Go monolith on ECS Fargate. Authentication is a hashed, tenant-scoped API key.\n3. Postgres 16 on RDS, Multi-AZ, with RLS **on**. One transaction writes `subscription`, the balanced `ledger_entries` and an `outbox` row.\n4. Outbox worker (same binary, worker mode). It creates the invoice and calls Stripe with an idempotency key of `invoice_id:attempt_n`.\n5. Stripe live mode.\n6. Webhook ingress `POST /webhooks/stripe`. It checks the signature, removes duplicates by `event.id`, writes the payment ledger entries and marks the invoice paid.\n\n**Deployed:** Terraform for all infrastructure. GitHub Actions builds **one** container image, identified by its digest, and promotes it from dev to staging to prod. Database migrations run through a versioned tool (Atlas or Flyway) before rollout. Rollback means redeploying the previous digest.\n\n**Logged:** Structured JSON logs. Every line carries `trace_id`, `tenant_id`, `idempotency_key` and `module`.\n\n**Monitored:**\n- OpenTelemetry traces cover the whole path: API, DB, outbox, worker, Stripe, webhook, DB. The webhook span links back to the original trace through the payment intent's metadata.\n- Request rate, errors and latency (RED metrics) per route.\n- An outbox-lag gauge.\n- A **ledger invariant check** every 5 minutes: debits must equal credits per tenant and currency. It pages on any imbalance.\n- An hourly synthetic canary that runs the whole flow in staging.\n\n**Exit check:** In prod, one real request produces a paid invoice. One trace spans every tier, the ledger invariant metric reads 0, and the canary passes. The refund also goes through and is recorded in the ledger.\n\n## 4. Phases (ordered by dependency; within a phase, widest blast radius first)\n\n### Phase 1: Tenancy and money foundation\n- **Unlocks:** Any real tenant and any real money record. Everything later writes into these structures.\n- **Depends on:** The Phase 0 skeleton running in prod, with RLS and the ledger invariant working on one tenant.\n- **Tasks (widest → narrowest):**\n  1. **Tenant isolation model:** `tenant_id` and an RLS policy on every table. A CI migration lint rejects any table missing either one. A cross-tenant test suite calls every repository function with the wrong tenant context and expects zero rows.\n  2. **Ledger schema hardened:** a chart of accounts per tenant (AR, cash, deferred revenue, revenue, credits, tax payable), an immutability trigger and the money type with its rounding policy.\n  3. **Idempotency framework:** an `Idempotency-Key` header on every mutating endpoint, with the stored response returned on retry.\n  4. **Billing account entity:** legal name, address, tax IDs, currency and billing contact. Tax and invoicing in Phase 3 depend on it.\n  5. **Authentication and authorization:** tenant API keys with scopes, plus internal operator roles (`billing-admin`, `finance-readonly`).\n  6. **Append-only audit log** of who changed what, with the before and after.\n  7. Read-only internal admin view of tenants and ledgers.\n- **Exit check:** The cross-tenant suite is green. Property-based tests with fixed seeds show that 100k random operations always leave the ledger balanced. Replaying 10k duplicate requests produces exactly one effect each. A point-in-time restore drill finishes within the 4 h RTO.\n\n### Phase 2: Catalog and subscriptions\n- **Unlocks:** Recurring charges. Invoices, usage pricing and the portal all reference these entities.\n- **Depends on:** Proven tenancy, ledger and idempotency (Phase 1).\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. **Price and plan data contract:** prices are versioned and **become immutable once any subscription uses them**. Every invoice line will point to a `price_version_id`.\n  2. **Subscription state machine:** `trialing → active → past_due → canceled | paused`. Only listed transitions are allowed, and each one posts its ledger entries in the same transaction.\n  3. **Billing-period engine:** a pure function of (anchor date, interval, clock) that handles month-end, leap years and the tenant's billing time zone. The clock is injected, never read from the wall.\n  4. **Proration:** daily in v1, with the calculation inputs stored next to the result.\n  5. Plan change, cancel and pause APIs.\n  6. Endpoint listing a tenant's plans.\n- **Exit check:** Golden-file tests pass for period calculations from 2024 to 2030, including Feb 29, the 31st→30th month change and DST. A model-based test of the state machine finds no illegal transition. Every subscription change leaves the ledger balanced.\n\n### Phase 3: Invoicing and tax\n- **Unlocks:** Legally valid bills. Payments need a finalized invoice to collect against.\n- **Depends on:** Subscriptions and billing periods (Phase 2) and billing accounts (Phase 1).\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. **Invoice data contract and numbering:** sequential numbers per tenant's legal entity, and invoices are **immutable after finalization** (enforced by trigger). Each line stores its source ledger entries and price version.\n  2. **Billing-run scheduler:** idempotent per (subscription, period) through a unique constraint. Each tenant is checkpointed and the run can resume. A failure in one tenant's run doesn't stop the others.\n  3. **Tax integration** (Stripe Tax or Avalara): the response is stored on the invoice, and an invoice is **never finalized without tax**. If the tax provider is down, the invoice stays a draft and is retried.\n  4. Credit notes and adjustments, recorded as reversing ledger entries.\n  5. PDF rendering, stored in S3 with signed URLs that expire.\n  6. Invoice emails.\n- **Exit check:** A shadow billing run over all subscriptions matches the ledger to the cent. Running the same period again creates **zero** new invoices. Killing the run partway through and restarting it gives identical output.\n\n### Phase 4: Payments and collections\n- **Unlocks:** Getting paid at scale and recovering failed payments.\n- **Depends on:** Immutable invoices that match the ledger (Phase 3), and the Stripe path proven in Phase 0.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. **Payment state machine and webhook ingestion contract:** signature check, duplicate removal by event ID, and safe handling of out-of-order events by fetching the latest state from Stripe instead of trusting the order events arrive in.\n  2. **Daily reconciliation:** Stripe balance transactions compared with ledger cash entries. Any difference that can't be explained pages someone.\n  3. **Retry and dunning policy:** jittered retry schedule, `past_due` transitions, grace period, and a hook to suspend the tenant's service.\n  4. Refunds. Refunds above a set amount need a second person's approval.\n  5. Payment-method update flow (Stripe Elements, with SCA and 3DS).\n  6. Payment-receipt emails.\n- **Exit check:** 14 straight days of reconciliation with zero unexplained differences on live traffic. A fault-injection suite passes: duplicate, reordered and 24 h-delayed webhooks all settle to the correct state, and a simulated processor outage leaves no double charges.\n\n### Phase 5: Usage metering and rating\n- **Unlocks:** Usage-based and hybrid pricing.\n- **Depends on:** The catalog's price versions (Phase 2), invoice lines (Phase 3) and collections (Phase 4). Usage priced onto an invoice that can't be collected is worthless, so this comes after.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. **Usage event schema contract:** `{tenant_id, meter, quantity, timestamp, idempotency_key, properties}`. Tenant clients integrate against this, so it is the hardest thing in the phase to change later. The other reading is a billing platform that other businesses use to charge their own customers. That version needs a second tenant level (merchant → end customer) and is hard to add later, so it's listed as a gate in §2 instead of being assumed.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Classification\n- **What:** A system that keeps the price catalog, manages subscriptions, meters usage, prices it, issues invoices, collects payments and runs retries on failed payments, for many tenants that share one platform.\n- **Type:** Software, plus infrastructure for usage ingestion. **No AI.**\n- **Dominant constraint:** **Correctness.** Money has to be exact, fully traceable and charged exactly once. Compliance comes second (PCI scope, tax, audit trail).\n- **Worst failure:** **Wrong money.** That means charging a tenant twice, using one tenant's data to bill another, or failing to record revenue without anyone noticing. All three destroy trust, and the third can go unseen for months.\n\n## 2. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Default (chosen now) | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Consistency vs availability** | **Split.** The ledger, invoices and payments need strong consistency: one Postgres primary, with ledger writes in serializable transactions. Usage ingestion stays available instead: it accepts events into a durable buffer even when the core database is down, and removes duplicates later. | Contractual multi-region active-active, or data residency rules. Answer with regional **cells**: each tenant is pinned to one region and keeps a consistent ledger there. Never use a globally distributed ledger. |\n| **Monolith vs services** | **Modular monolith.** One deployable with strict module boundaries (tenancy, catalog, subscriptions, metering, rating, invoicing, ledger, payments, dunning) and one Postgres. Modules talk only through their public interfaces, and a CI lint blocks imports across modules. | Usage ingestion stays above about 5k events/s, or ingestion deploys start blocking core billing deploys. Then split out **metering only**. Also flip when there are 3 or more teams with clashing release schedules. |\n| **Sync vs async** | **Sync** for API changes such as creating a subscription or changing a plan: the state change and its ledger entries go in one transaction. **Async**, through a transactional outbox, for billing runs, payment attempts, tax calls, emails and webhooks. Postgres `SKIP LOCKED` workers to start; no Kafka. | Checkout needs payment confirmation inline (for example a strict SCA flow). Then add a sync charge path for that endpoint only. Move to a broker when 3 or more independent consumers need fan-out and replay. |\n| **Build vs buy** | **Buy** payment processing (Stripe Payments with Elements, so cards never reach us and PCI scope stays at SAQ-A), tax (Stripe Tax or Avalara) and email (Postmark or SES). **Build** the ledger, subscriptions, rating and invoicing. The ledger is the source of truth, usage pricing will outgrow off-the-shelf models, and we don't want to depend on one processor. | If the real pricing sheet is only flat per-seat plans with no usage pricing, **buy the whole engine** (Stripe Billing, Chargebee or Orb). This plan then shrinks to integration plus a ledger copy. **Check this against the actual pricing sheet in week 1.** |\n| **Tenant isolation model** | **Shared database and shared schema.** Every row has `tenant_id`, enforced by **Postgres row-level security (RLS)** using a per-transaction `app.tenant_id` setting. The app's database role is not the table owner, so it cannot bypass RLS. | An enterprise contract requires a dedicated database, or a tenant creates noisy-neighbor load. Then move that tenant into a dedicated cell with the same schema and migrations. |\n| **Ledger model** | **Double-entry, append-only and immutable.** Corrections are made with reversing entries, never `UPDATE` or `DELETE` (a database trigger enforces this). Normal state tables sit beside it; this is not full event sourcing. | **Treat this as permanent.** The only flip is to full event sourcing, if a regulator or auditor needs every state rebuilt from scratch. |\n| **Money representation** | `bigint` minor units plus an ISO 4217 currency code. No floats anywhere. Rounding rules (banker's or half-up, per currency) live in one place. Each price list is set in one currency; **no FX conversion**. | A tenant must be billed in a currency that has no price list. Then add an FX rate table and record the rate used on each invoice. |\n| **Tenant hierarchy** | One level: **tenant = billed customer**, with billing accounts below it. | We sell billing to other businesses. Then add a merchant → customer hierarchy with per-merchant processor accounts (Stripe Connect). Decide this before Phase 1 because every table changes. |\n| **Region / residency** | Single region (for example `us-east-1`) spread across zones. RPO 5 min or less, RTO 4 h or less. | The first EU-residency contract, or a region-level RTO under 1 h. Then add an EU cell. |\n| **(AI) prompt+RAG vs fine-tune** | N/A: there are no model-driven features. | An AI feature is proposed. Re-run this skill for that feature. |\n| **(AI) hosted API vs self-host** | N/A, same reason. | Same. |\n\n## 3. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n\n**The one real request:** `POST /v1/subscriptions` for one internal tenant (`acme-internal`) on one hard-coded plan (`starter`, $1.00/month, USD), followed by a real live-mode charge to a company card. The charge is refunded afterwards.\n\n**Real response:** `201` with the subscription ID. Then, asynchronously: invoice `INV-0001` is finalized, Stripe charges $1.00, the `payment_intent.succeeded` webhook comes back, and the invoice is marked `paid`. The ledger ends up balanced: accounts receivable, cash and deferred revenue entries net to zero.\n\n**Tiers it crosses:**\n1. Edge: ALB with TLS and AWS WAF.\n2. API: Go monolith on ECS Fargate. Authentication is a hashed, tenant-scoped API key.\n3. Postgres 16 on RDS, Multi-AZ, with RLS **on**. One transaction writes `subscription`, the balanced `ledger_entries` and an `outbox` row.\n4. Outbox worker (same binary, worker mode). It creates the invoice and calls Stripe with an idempotency key of `invoice_id:attempt_n`.\n5. Stripe live mode.\n6. Webhook ingress `POST /webhooks/stripe`. It checks the signature, removes duplicates by `event.id`, writes the payment ledger entries and marks the invoice paid.\n\n**Deployed:** Terraform for all infrastructure. GitHub Actions builds **one** container image, identified by its digest, and promotes it from dev to staging to prod. Database migrations run through a versioned tool (Atlas or Flyway) before rollout. Rollback means redeploying the previous digest.\n\n**Logged:** Structured JSON logs. Every line carries `trace_id`, `tenant_id`, `idempotency_key` and `module`.\n\n**Monitored:**\n- OpenTelemetry traces cover the whole path: API, DB, outbox, worker, Stripe, webhook, DB. The webhook span links back to the original trace through the payment intent's metadata.\n- Request rate, errors and latency (RED metrics) per route.\n- An outbox-lag gauge.\n- A **ledger invariant check** every 5 minutes: debits must equal credits per tenant and currency. It pages on any imbalance.\n- An hourly synthetic canary that runs the whole flow in staging.\n\n**Exit check:** In prod, one real request produces a paid invoice. One trace spans every tier, the ledger invariant metric reads 0, and the canary passes. The refund also goes through and is recorded in the ledger.\n\n## 4. Phases (ordered by dependency; within a phase, widest blast radius first)\n\n### Phase 1: Tenancy and money foundation\n- **Unlocks:** Any real tenant and any real money record. Everything later writes into these structures.\n- **Depends on:** The Phase 0 skeleton running in prod, with RLS and the ledger invariant working on one tenant.\n- **Tasks (widest → narrowest):**\n  1. **Tenant isolation model:** `tenant_id` and an RLS policy on every table. A CI migration lint rejects any table missing either one. A cross-tenant test suite calls every repository function with the wrong tenant context and expects zero rows.\n  2. **Ledger schema hardened:** a chart of accounts per tenant (AR, cash, deferred revenue, revenue, credits, tax payable), an immutability trigger and the money type with its rounding policy.\n  3. **Idempotency framework:** an `Idempotency-Key` header on every mutating endpoint, with the stored response returned on retry.\n  4. **Billing account entity:** legal name, address, tax IDs, currency and billing contact. Tax and invoicing in Phase 3 depend on it.\n  5. **Authentication and authorization:** tenant API keys with scopes, plus internal operator roles (`billing-admin`, `finance-readonly`).\n  6. **Append-only audit log** of who changed what, with the before and after.\n  7. Read-only internal admin view of tenants and ledgers.\n- **Exit check:** The cross-tenant suite is green. Property-based tests with fixed seeds show that 100k random operations always leave the ledger balanced. Replaying 10k duplicate requests produces exactly one effect each. A point-in-time restore drill finishes within the 4 h RTO.\n\n### Phase 2: Catalog and subscriptions\n- **Unlocks:** Recurring charges. Invoices, usage pricing and the portal all reference these entities.\n- **Depends on:** Proven tenancy, ledger and idempotency (Phase 1).\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. **Price and plan data contract:** prices are versioned and **become immutable once any subscription uses them**. Every invoice line will point to a `price_version_id`.\n  2. **Subscription state machine:** `trialing → active → past_due → canceled | paused`. Only listed transitions are allowed, and each one posts its ledger entries in the same transaction.\n  3. **Billing-period engine:** a pure function of (anchor date, interval, clock) that handles month-end, leap years and the tenant's billing time zone. The clock is injected, never read from the wall.\n  4. **Proration:** daily in v1, with the calculation inputs stored next to the result.\n  5. Plan change, cancel and pause APIs.\n  6. Endpoint listing a tenant's plans.\n- **Exit check:** Golden-file tests pass for period calculations from 2024 to 2030, including Feb 29, the 31st→30th month change and DST. A model-based test of the state machine finds no illegal transition. Every subscription change leaves the ledger balanced.\n\n### Phase 3: Invoicing and tax\n- **Unlocks:** Legally valid bills. Payments need a finalized invoice to collect against.\n- **Depends on:** Subscriptions and billing periods (Phase 2) and billing accounts (Phase 1).\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. **Invoice data contract and numbering:** sequential numbers per tenant's legal entity, and invoices are **immutable after finalization** (enforced by trigger). Each line stores its source ledger entries and price version.\n  2. **Billing-run scheduler:** idempotent per (subscription, period) through a unique constraint. Each tenant is checkpointed and the run can resume. A failure in one tenant's run doesn't stop the others.\n  3. **Tax integration** (Stripe Tax or Avalara): the response is stored on the invoice, and an invoice is **never finalized without tax**. If the tax provider is down, the invoice stays a draft and is retried.\n  4. Credit notes and adjustments, recorded as reversing ledger entries.\n  5. PDF rendering, stored in S3 with signed URLs that expire.\n  6. Invoice emails.\n- **Exit check:** A shadow billing run over all subscriptions matches the ledger to the cent. Running the same period again creates **zero** new invoices. Killing the run partway through and restarting it gives identical output.\n\n### Phase 4: Payments and collections\n- **Unlocks:** Getting paid at scale and recovering failed payments.\n- **Depends on:** Immutable invoices that match the ledger (Phase 3), and the Stripe path proven in Phase 0.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. **Payment state machine and webhook ingestion contract:** signature check, duplicate removal by event ID, and safe handling of out-of-order events by fetching the latest state from Stripe instead of trusting the order events arrive in.\n  2. **Daily reconciliation:** Stripe balance transactions compared with ledger cash entries. Any difference that can't be explained pages someone.\n  3. **Retry and dunning policy:** jittered retry schedule, `past_due` transitions, grace period, and a hook to suspend the tenant's service.\n  4. Refunds. Refunds above a set amount need a second person's approval.\n  5. Payment-method update flow (Stripe Elements, with SCA and 3DS).\n  6. Payment-receipt emails.\n- **Exit check:** 14 straight days of reconciliation with zero unexplained differences on live traffic. A fault-injection suite passes: duplicate, reordered and 24 h-delayed webhooks all settle to the correct state, and a simulated processor outage leaves no double charges.\n\n### Phase 5: Usage metering and rating\n- **Unlocks:** Usage-based and hybrid pricing.\n- **Depends on:** The catalog's price versions (Phase 2), invoice lines (Phase 3) and collections (Phase 4). Usage priced onto an invoice that can't be collected is worthless, so this comes after.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. **Usage event schema contract:** `{tenant_id, meter, quantity, timestamp, idempotency_key, properties}`. Events that arrive later go into the next invoice as adjustments.\n  4. **Pricing models** (tiered, volume, package, overage), versioned, as a pure function of (aggregates, price version).\n  5. Usage lines added to the billing run.\n  6. Usage-to-date preview API.\n- **Exit check:** Replaying the raw event log for a closed period gives **identical** priced totals. A load test at 10x the expected peak passes. Ingestion keeps accepting events during a 30-minute database outage and loses none.\n\n### Phase 6: Tenant- and operator-facing features (the visible parts, built last)\n- **Unlocks:** Self-serve billing, finance workflows and integrations.\n- **Depends on:** All billing data being correct and reconciled (Phases 1–5).\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. **Outbound event and webhook contract for tenants:** `invoice.finalized`, `payment.failed` and others. External systems build against it.\n  2. **Accounting export:** mapping our ledger accounts to the general ledger in NetSuite or QuickBooks.\n  3. Operator adjustment tooling, which needs a second person's approval.\n  4. Revenue reporting: MRR, ARR, deferred revenue and churn.\n  5. Customer billing portal: invoices, payment methods, plan changes, usage.\n  6. Dashboard polish.\n- **Exit check:** Finance closes one month entirely from the export with no manual fixes. Outbound webhook delivery is at least 99.9% with retries. The portal's numbers match the ledger exactly in an automated comparison.\n\n## 5.
